{"id": "35:18/q04", "question": "What is the grammar of wāzirah and muthqalah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q04/p1", "position": "Both feminine adjectives imply nafs, which can mean a male or female person.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and al-Farrāʾ cite 3:185; Naḥḥās mentions dābba and al-Akhfash's insān; Islahi notes common ellipsis; Abū Ḥayyān explains the later masculine pronoun by the sense 'person'."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q05", "question": "How is taziru formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q05/p1", "position": "Its original initial wāw was deleted in the pattern of yaziru.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Qurṭubī give tawzaru as the underlying form."}, {"id": "35:18/q05/p2", "position": "Its indicative form states a prohibition.", "reasons": "Jishumī says declarative syntax has prohibitive force."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q06", "question": "What prompted the burden rule according to the reported occasion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q06/p1", "position": "Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra urged believers to reject Muhammad and promised to bear their sins.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya states the occasion; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī report it; Zamakhsharī cites the promise in 29:12."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q07", "question": "How does this rule apply to misleaders' added burdens?", "turns_on": "Whether extra burdens are the person's own causal sin or another burden imposed unwillingly.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q07/p1", "position": "The added load is their own sin of misleading, while followers remain liable for their own choice.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Kuran Yolu, and Study Quran reconcile 29:12–13. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Elmalılı cite the hadith on originating practices."}, {"id": "35:18/q07/p2", "position": "Additional burdens are imposed unwillingly; this verse denies carrying another's sin willingly.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl offers this reconciliation."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q08", "question": "Can a relative be punished for someone's crime in worldly law?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q08/p1", "position": "Only if the relative aided, supported, knew of, or approved the crime and so shared responsibility.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya states this; Abū Ḥayyān reports it and condemns punishment of innocent associates."}, {"id": "35:18/q08/p2", "position": "The rule supplies a maxim of personal legal responsibility.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu says early Muslim jurists used it and compares Western law's later adoption."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q09", "question": "What is a muthqalah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q09/p1", "position": "A soul weighed down by sins.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, and later exegetes give this sense; Bursevī cites al-Rāghib on literal heaviness extended to sin and debt; Biqāʿī includes disbelief."}, {"id": "35:18/q09/p2", "position": "The feminine wording heightens the expectation of mercy.", "reasons": "Jishumī says women are seen as weaker and likelier to receive help, yet none is given."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q10", "question": "What happens when a burdened soul asks for help?", "turns_on": "Whether ilā ḥimlihā names the load itself or the burden of carrying it.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q10/p1", "position": "No one takes any part of its sins, even after a plea, whether kin or stranger.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatāda, and many later authors say the refusal is total. Rāzī says even a severe load and plea win no relief; Biqāʿī and Elmalılı include voluntary and forced transfer; Islahi says the righteous did not share the wrongdoing."}, {"id": "35:18/q10/p2", "position": "The call may be construed as asking someone to bear the burden of its load.", "reasons": "Ālūsī transmits this alternative sense of ilā ḥimlihā."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q11", "question": "Why is the call for help so pointed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q11/p1", "position": "It evokes a desperate rescue call that would normally stir sympathy.", "reasons": "Rāzī says an overwhelmed person finally asks after silent endurance; Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes Arab rescue custom, Waddāk's verse, and a proverb about generosity even to death."}, {"id": "35:18/q11/p2", "position": "It restates the first rule in a more urgent scene.", "reasons": "Mujāhid explicitly equates the clauses; Elmalılı reads a hint at attempts to shift sin."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q12", "question": "What does ḥiml mean and what does its pronoun refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q12/p1", "position": "A physical load carried on the back, metaphorically the soul's sins.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares hands metaphorically earning deeds; al-Kisāʾī and Ibn al-Sikkīt distinguish pronunciations for back load, pregnancy, and palm fruit; al-Mufradāt distinguishes external ḥiml from internal ḥaml."}, {"id": "35:18/q12/p2", "position": "The pronoun in 'none of it' points to the soul's burden.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī specifies its antecedent."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q13", "question": "What is omitted in the call's construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q13/p1", "position": "The object called upon is implicit, making the statement cover any possible helper.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and Zamakhsharī supply the person; Ibn ʿĀshūr also supplies an implied request for carrying as the aim of ilā; Islahi notes an omitted governing noun."}, {"id": "35:18/q13/p2", "position": "The feminine verb's subject is the implied soul.", "reasons": "Bursevī points out its feminine singular form."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q14", "question": "What are the readings of lā yuḥmal and shayʾ?", "turns_on": "Passive versus active verb and nominative versus accusative shayʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q14/p1", "position": "The common passive has shayʾ as deputy subject.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn records it."}, {"id": "35:18/q14/p2", "position": "An active reading has the summoned person as subject and shayʾan as object.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn attributes it to Abū al-Simmāl, Ṭalḥa, and al-Kisāʾī; Ālūsī specifies tāʾ and kasra on mīm in reports."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q15", "question": "Who is the close relative?", "turns_on": "Whether kāna's implicit subject is the helper or the caller.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q15/p1", "position": "The summoned helper is kin to the burdened soul.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Ṭabarī, Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr favor or use this reading; examples are parent, child, sibling, or spouse. Rāzī says kinship makes refusal more striking."}, {"id": "35:18/q15/p2", "position": "The caller is kin to the person asked.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives this alternative; Abū Ḥayyān defends its coherence; al-Samīn and Biqāʿī allow both."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q16", "question": "How does kāna work in 'even if a close relative'?", "turns_on": "Which implied subject and case are read, and whether kāna is complete.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q16/p1", "position": "Kāna is incomplete, with an omitted person as subject and dhā qurbā as predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and Ṭabarī parse the predicate; Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, and Ālūsī prefer the summoned helper as subject because the syntax and sense hold together."}, {"id": "35:18/q16/p2", "position": "The omitted subject is instead the caller.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives this parse; Abū Ḥayyān finds it coherent."}, {"id": "35:18/q16/p3", "position": "With nominative dhū qurbā, kāna may be complete or have an omitted predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Sībawayh permit it, citing a hardship verse and an elliptical reward example; al-Samīn cites 2:280. Zamakhsharī and Bayḍāwī object to the complete-verb analysis."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q17", "question": "What scenes of family refusal are reported?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in who asks, what is asked, and any limited relief.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q17/p1", "position": "A parent asks a child to bear sins; the child refuses because of its own burden.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is transmitted by Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ṭabrisī, and Bursevī; Bursevī adds a husband's request for a speck of merit from his wife."}, {"id": "35:18/q17/p2", "position": "A mother invokes pregnancy, nursing, and care to ask a son to bear one sin; he refuses.", "reasons": "Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ is reported by Thaʿlabī and Qurṭubī."}, {"id": "35:18/q17/p3", "position": "Neighbors, Jews or Christians, parents, children, and spouses plead at Judgment; each fears for their own fate.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima's accounts differ in speakers and requests; some include a believer's appeal that reduces an unbeliever's place in Hell, without transfer of sin."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q18", "question": "Does the refusal rule exclude every intercession?", "turns_on": "Whether God-permitted mitigation amounts to transferring another's sin.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q18/p1", "position": "It excludes family or patronage as independent rescue and excludes transferring personal guilt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists imagined autonomous intercessors; Kuran Yolu says they projected worldly patronage; Elmalılı cites 2:123 and 14:31."}, {"id": "35:18/q18/p2", "position": "Intercession by God's permission or divinely granted expiation can occur.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr names Muhammad's intercession and believing children for bereaved mothers, citing 34:23; ʿIkrima reports partial easing of an unbeliever's punishment."}]}

{"id": "35:18/q22", "question": "What does innamā convey?", "turns_on": "Absolute versus context-relative restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q22/p1", "position": "It restricts effective warning to the receptive and indirectly reproaches the obstinate.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says innamā has more force than merely making inna inoperative; Burhān compares the unreceptive to people without hearing or reason; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the restriction qasr qalb."}, {"id": "35:18/q22/p2", "position": "Literal exclusivity is also possible.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr acknowledges it but favors a context-relative correction."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q23", "question": "Who are those described as fearing and praying?", "turns_on": "General believers or particular early recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q23/p1", "position": "Sincere believers or Muslims who receive warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says description instead of a group name praises their belief and practice; Qatāda contrasts living believers with dead-hearted unbelievers."}, {"id": "35:18/q23/p2", "position": "The Prophet's Companions in particular.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī identifies their lasting fear and prayer."}, {"id": "35:18/q23/p3", "position": "God's allies who fear unseen punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported by Wāḥidī."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q24", "question": "What does bil-ghayb refer to?", "turns_on": "What is unseen: God, observers, punishment, the Prophet, or unseen reality.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q24/p1", "position": "God, whom they fear without seeing.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and Elmalılı give this sense."}, {"id": "35:18/q24/p2", "position": "Their private state: they fear unseen by other people.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Māwardī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and others emphasize inward sincerity; Biqāʿī invokes Khadīja and al-Ṣiddīq."}, {"id": "35:18/q24/p3", "position": "God's punishment, the Fire, reckoning, or afterlife, still unseen to them.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAbbās name unseen judgment; Qatāda names Fire and reckoning; Ibn ʿĪsā and Jishumī stress afterlife belief."}, {"id": "35:18/q24/p4", "position": "The absent Prophet who communicates by a message.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives this reading."}, {"id": "35:18/q24/p5", "position": "Unseen realities in general.", "reasons": "Asad cites 2:3, 27:80–81 and 30:52–53."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q25", "question": "How is bil-ghayb parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q25/p1", "position": "It may be circumstantial of the fearer or of what is feared.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Nasafī, al-Samīn, Bursevī, and Ālūsī set out both attachments."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q26", "question": "What does establishing prayer require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q26/p1", "position": "Maintaining prescribed prayer properly, with its times and conditions.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā specify the obligatory prayer; Ṭabrisī its conditions; Nasafī its times; Biqāʿī the five prayers and sunnas; Ibn ʿĀshūr says none is neglected."}, {"id": "35:18/q26/p2", "position": "Making prayer an enduring raised standard.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Bursevī, and Ālūsī use this image."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q27", "question": "Why pair fear with prayer and use different verb forms?", "turns_on": "Verbal aspect and prayer's thematic prominence.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q27/p1", "position": "Fear is continuous, while prayer has fixed recurring times.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī, Biqāʿī, and Kashf al-Asrār via Bursevī explain present versus past this way; Bayḍāwī sees enduring practice; Ālūsī refers to 35:9."}, {"id": "35:18/q27/p2", "position": "Prayer is the foremost outward sign of inward fear and deserves particular honor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is singled out for honor; Rāzī compares inward faith with outward deeds; Biqāʿī calls prayer noblest worship; Tabāṭabāʾī and Islahi stress its centrality."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q28", "question": "What follows from the emphasis on prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q28/p1", "position": "A profession of faith without prayer or practice does not benefit a person.", "reasons": "Jishumī argues against the Murjiʾa; Bursevī cites a hadith on abandoning prayer and unbelief; Islahi says neglect betrays heedlessness."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q29", "question": "What is tazakkā?", "turns_on": "Whether purification is glossed as good deeds, cleansing sin, or finding guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q29/p1", "position": "Reforming oneself through obedience and righteous works.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Qatāda, Muqātil, Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, and others include doing good; Ṭabrisī includes zakat and duties; Biqāʿī stresses effort against the soul's pull; Kuran Yolu includes avoiding prohibitions."}, {"id": "35:18/q29/p2", "position": "Cleansing disbelief, sins, idolatry, or indecency through repentance and faith.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī names repentance, faith and obedience; Ibn al-Jawzī adds idolatry; Bayḍāwī calls sin a stain; Ālūsī says warning prompts purification."}, {"id": "35:18/q29/p3", "position": "Finding guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās via Wāḥidī and Qurṭubī gives this gloss."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q30", "question": "How is the purification clause read?", "turns_on": "Retained versus assimilated tāʾ and variant initial hamza.", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q30/p1", "position": "The common wording retains the tāʾ of tafaʿʿul.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān identify the majority reading."}, {"id": "35:18/q30/p2", "position": "Other readings assimilate tāʾ into zāy, some with an initial connecting hamza.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿūd and Ṭalḥa are named by al-Samīn, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī; Kashshāf, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī and Qurṭubī give related forms."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q31", "question": "Who benefits from purification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q31/p1", "position": "The benefit and reward return to the person who purifies, while sin harms its doer.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī names God's pleasure, Paradise and escape from punishment; Biqāʿī and Ālūsī draw the reverse implication for sin; Tabāṭabāʾī and Islahi say God needs no worship; Ibn ʿĀshūr says accepting warning benefits its hearer."}, {"id": "35:18/q31/p2", "position": "Reward and punishment follow human agents' own deeds.", "reasons": "Jishumī argues against the Mujbira and the claim that human acts are created."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q32", "question": "How does the purification maxim serve the passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q32/p1", "position": "It generalizes fear and prayer as purification and encourages it with personal reward.", "reasons": "Rāzī links it to nontransferable sin; Ibn ʿAṭiyya sees strong hope; Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī, Tabāṭabāʾī and Ibn ʿĀshūr include the preceding traits; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it proverbial tadhyīl."}, {"id": "35:18/q32/p2", "position": "It balances the personal stain of sin against the personal growth of virtue.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī supplies the implicit contrast; Bursevī likens obedience to light at the crossing that another cannot share."}]}
{"id": "35:18/q33", "question": "What does the return to God mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:18/q33/p1", "position": "All return to God for judgment and recompense of their deeds.", "reasons": "Rāzī says hidden consequences become visible then; Ibn ʿĀshūr says fronting 'to God' draws attention to divine justice and generosity and serves the cadence; Bursevī includes Paradise and divine beauty."}, {"id": "35:18/q33/p2", "position": "It warns the unpurified and promises reward to those purified.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses warning; Kashshāf and Nasafī stress reward."}]}

{"id": "35:22/q01", "question": "Who or what are the living and the dead?", "turns_on": "Whether life and death primarily name faith and disbelief, knowledge and ignorance, broader spiritual states, Sufi realization, or the image's literal sensory contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q01/p1", "position": "The living are believers, and the dead are disbelievers, whose hearts and actions lack the life of faith.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Tabari, Qatada, and others explain that believers know, see, act, and respond while disbelievers do not benefit from revelation. Yahya, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur, al-Tabatabai, and the Study Quran cite 6:122; al-Wahidi's Ibn Abbas cites 16:21; Ibn Kathir adds 11:24, and the Study Quran adds 39:22. Ibn Abbas in al-Tabari maps the wider images to obedience and disobedience; in al-Nahhas he maps them to belief, error, Paradise, and Fire. {"id": "35:22/q02", "question": "Why is the living and dead contrast stronger than the earlier comparisons?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q02/p1", "position": "The dead lack the useful perception that even a blind living person retains, so the last comparison intensifies the difference.", "reasons": "Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, al-Biqai, al-Alusi's Imam, and Kuranyolu argue that a blind person shares some cognition with a sighted one, whereas the dead differ from the living in perception or very reality. {"id": "35:22/q03", "question": "Why are the living and dead plural here?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural itself stresses the universal disparity or varies the class expression for referents and cadence.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q03/p1", "position": "The plural underscores an absolute difference between every living person and every dead person.", "reasons": "Al-Razi and al-Samin say no dead individual equals any living individual in perception, whether comparing kinds or individuals; al-Bursevi links the plurals with the stronger contrast."}, {"id": "35:22/q03/p2", "position": "The plural marks multiple referents, while earlier singulars express generic classes or preserve cadence.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says blind and sighted are singular for generic class and verse ending. {"id": "35:22/q06", "question": "What is the force of لا in this and the preceding comparisons?", "turns_on": "Whether la is emphatic surplus or an operative negation requiring reconstruction of the paired comparisons.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q06/p1", "position": "It is extra or emphatic, reinforcing the denial that the paired opposites are equal.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash in al-Nahhas treats it as extra; al-Nasafi and al-Tabatabai say repetition strengthens negation. {"id": "35:22/q07", "question": "What does God making someone hear mean?", "turns_on": "Whether hearing here denotes audible perception itself or the further understanding and acceptance that benefits the hearer.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q07/p1", "position": "God grants receptive hearing: understanding, guidance, admonition, and a response to faith.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls the object faith; Yahya, al-Wahidi's al-Suddi, al-Durr's al-Suddi, and al-Biqai call it guidance. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, and others add taking heed, accepting proof, and submission. Ibn Jawzi says understanding; al-Khafaji in al-Alusi says attentive acceptance and reflection. Ibn Ashur connects this to a prepared heart and the restriction of useful warning in 35:18. Al-Islahi glosses the causative as urging and propelling to listen and accept; al-Tabatabai speaks of reviving a receptive believer, citing 6:122; the Study Quran cites 30:52–53."}, {"id": "35:22/q07/p2", "position": "The causative can mean producing an audible sound that a listener can perceive, or enabling perception of that sound.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi defines ismaʿ as making an audible, perceptible sound and samʿ as perception or the ear itself. Al-Tabrisi gives the same account of ismaʿ. Al-Alusi says God enables perception of sounds; al-Tabrisi specifies that literal hearing by unbelievers is compatible with their failure to benefit."}]}
{"id": "35:22/q08", "question": "Whom does God choose to make hear, and on what basis?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes specify divine choice alone, prior protection for Paradise, or a human readiness preserved under God's wisdom.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q08/p1", "position": "God freely grants guidance and effective hearing to whomever He wills; identical outward access to the message does not determine response.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya returns hearing to God's will. {"id": "35:22/q09", "question": "Whom can the Prophet not make hear, and what does that inability mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause chiefly describes unreceptive disbelievers or distinguishes God's power to confer hearing from the Prophet's own ability.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q09/p1", "position": "He cannot make stubborn disbelievers benefit from or accept the message, just as the buried dead do not answer a summons.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, and others explain the grave simile as failure to heed scripture, proofs, and warning. Al-Baydawi and al-Bursevi say the expression extends the metaphor and discourages hope of conversion. Al-Biqai stresses that even extraordinary signs bring no benefit. Ibn Ashur says these are people God did not will to hear, and al-Islahi describes the Prophet's worry over his people's indifference."}, {"id": "35:22/q09/p2", "position": "God may make even the physically dead hear, but the Prophet cannot do so by himself; the analogy also relieves him of responsibility for conversion.", "reasons": "Al-Razi offers this as one reading, then alternatively says God alone could make even deaf rocks hear. Al-Tabatabai calls the Prophet an instrument of guidance."}]}

{"id": "35:22/q11", "question": "Can the dead literally hear, and how does this verse bear on the Badr report?", "turns_on": "Whether the Badr address involved actual hearing by the slain, exceptional restoration or disembodied hearing, or only a reproach directed at living unbelievers.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q11/p1", "position": "Ordinary dead people do not hear the living, but God may restore spirits or grant an exceptional hearing, including at Badr.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says faithful spirits are reported in trees near the Throne or lamps, unbelieving spirits in Sijjin, and spirits may sometimes approach graves and hear; he cites footsteps and Badr. {"id": "35:22/q15", "question": "How do the surrounding contrasts lead into this verse?", "turns_on": "How the commentators describe the sequence's organizing function: mapped opposites and consequences, or repeated examples of different human responses.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q15/p1", "position": "The sequence contrasts believers and disbelievers, faith and unbelief, and their consequences, culminating in life and death.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Samin, Ibn Ashur, al-Tabatabai, Kuranyolu, and Study Quran connect the pairs of sight, light, shade, and life with believers, and blindness, darkness, heat, and death with unbelievers. Ibn Kathir adds believers' gardens and disbelievers' burning wind, boiling water, and smoky shade (56:43–44); Kuranyolu gives ease versus hardship and fire. Ibn Ashur sees alternating comparisons of people and states, with a parallel sequence in 13:16. Al-Nasafi says conjunctions pair even with even and odd with odd. Al-Alusi traces the analogies back to the two seas of 35:12. Al-Nahhas transmits Ibn Abbas's assignments and notes that harur, unlike one proposed distinction from samum, may occur by day or night because its intensive form means harmful heat."}, {"id": "35:22/q15/p2", "position": "The passage also repeats explicit comparisons as a rhetorical pattern, moving through nature to show unlike human responses.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan notes the explicit comparisons unlike examples that leave subjects unnamed, and elsewhere calls the paired contrasts repeated comparisons. Al-Itqan similarly cites 35:19–22 as repeated examples. Al-Islahi compares Qur'anic rain received by fertile land but wasted on barren land and says God created natural opposites for the universe's benefit while giving respite to virtuous and vicious inclinations."}]}
{"id": "35:22/q16", "question": "How does the hearing clause connect to the preceding warning and the Prophet's task?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q16/p1", "position": "It explains why warning benefits only receptive people and consoles the Prophet: he must deliver the message, while God enables its acceptance.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai and Ibn Ashur relate selective hearing to 35:18. Ibn Ashur says the hearing clauses answer the prior comparison in matching order and excuse the Prophet's duty to preach to both groups. Al-Razi offers consolation as a reading: even deaf rocks would hear only through God. Al-Nasafi says the Prophet strains over people whose fate is hidden from him. Al-Islahi says the Prophet worried his people's indifference meant he had failed, though he must address the living and leave the dead to God; he says truth reaches wrongdoers conclusively while righteous people refine capacities."}]}
{"id": "35:22/q17", "question": "What further theological point do the verse's contrasts support?", "turns_on": "Which larger doctrinal implication is drawn from the contrast: divine sovereignty and exclusion of partners, or resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "35:22/q17/p1", "position": "They display God's free agency and exclude partners from His power and wise judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says unlike created states reveal God's unrestricted agency and that nothing resembles Him. {"id": "35:28/q01", "question": "How do people and animals vary in color?", "turns_on": "Whether the analogy extends from visible color to inward states.", "positions": [{"id": "35:28/q01/p1", "position": "They have diverse colors, like the fruits and mountains mentioned before.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari and Ibn Abbas list white, red, yellow and black; Qatada also lists green fruits and mountain tracks.
